items.text: A relational database is the default. Select another type when you can say what it cannot do.
Each piece of data has one main store. A cache or a search index is a copy.
One service or module writes each store. Others ask the owner.
Keep data that must change together in one database. Transactions there are cheap and reliable.
Make the CAP choice for each kind of data, not once for the whole system.
For eventual consistency, say which data can be old, for how long, and what the user sees.
Other users can see the half-done state of a saga. Show it as a real "pending" state.
An outbox can publish an event more than once. Receivers must tolerate repeats.
PostgreSQL, Oracle, and SQL Server default to read committed. Write down the level each critical transaction needs.
A copy of another service's data is read-only. Only the owner writes to it.
A cache must never be the only place where data lives.
When the cache stops, the database must survive the full load for a short time.
Analytical tools must never read a service database. Use events, a published view, or a data product.
When a popular entry expires, let only one request rebuild it. The others wait or get the old value.
Use a time limit as a safety net, and removal on change where fresh data matters.
A stopped pipeline shows old data as current. Add freshness checks that alert.
Select a partition key that keeps one request in one partition and spreads the load evenly.
Watch for hot keys. One famous account or popular event can overload its partition.
A cache key must contain every input that changes the answer, such as language or region.
Do not select a server by "hash mod n". A change of n moves almost every key.
